cr.missShot: You missed a winning shot. After {b} you would have been ahead once the captures were over.
cr.allowShot: This move let the opponent win material (after the exchanges you are a piece down). {b} would have prevented it.
cr.missKing: You missed a chance to crown a king. Best was {b}.

cr.backRank: This gave up your back-rank guard too early. Best was {b}.
cr.tip.goodShot: 💡 Giving one piece to take two — the "shot" — is the most important tactic in checkers.
cr.tip.missShot: 💡 Before you move, ask: "If I give a piece here, can I then jump several?"
cr.tip.allowShot: 💡 Before moving, check whether you leave an empty landing square behind your pieces. Captures are compulsory, so you can also be forced into one.
cr.tip.missKing: 💡 Kings can also move backwards — they are much stronger than men.
cr.tip.allowKing: 💡 A gap in your back row is where enemy men come through to be crowned.
cr.tip.backRank: 💡 In the opening and middlegame, keeping your back-row men (1 and 3 for Black, 30 and 32 for White) makes it hard for the opponent to crown.
cr.tip.gen: 💡 On the board, the arrow is the best move and the numbers are the value of moving to each square.
rl.title: Learn the rules
intro.hist: The game is believed to have begun in southern France around the 12th century, when the pieces of the old game alquerque were played on a chessboard. In Britain it is called draughts, and in 1756 William Payne published a book on its rules and tactics.
intro.win: Win by capturing all of your opponent's pieces or leaving them no legal move. Pieces move diagonally and capture by jumping over an enemy piece (when you can capture, you must).
intro.cult: It is "checkers" in the USA and "draughts" in Britain. International draughts on a 10×10 board is popular in the Netherlands and elsewhere, and Russian shashki on 64 squares in Russia. In 1994 the Canadian program Chinook became world champion in play against humans, and in 2007 it was proven that perfect play by both sides leads to a draw.
tr.board.b: Only the 32 dark squares of the 8×8 board are used. Black and White each start with 12 pieces on the three rows nearest to them. Black moves first. The squares are numbered 1–32, and moves are written with these numbers, like "11-15".
tr.move.b: Every piece starts as a "man". A man moves one square diagonally forward. It can never move backwards.
tr.move.task: Move one of the white men diagonally forward.
tr.move.ok: That's it! Men move forward one diagonal square at a time.
tr.jump.b: If an enemy piece is diagonally in front of you and the square behind it is empty, you jump over it and capture it. The captured piece is removed from the board.
tr.jump.task: Jump over the black piece to capture it.
tr.jump.ng: When you can capture, you must.
tr.must.b: When you can capture, you must capture — no other move is allowed. Players sometimes give a piece on purpose to force a capture, so always check whether a capture is possible.
tr.must.task: Find the capture and take it (no other piece may move).
tr.must.ok: Right! A capture always comes before any other move.
tr.multi.b: If, after a jump, you can jump another piece from the landing square, you keep jumping. One move can take several pieces, and you must keep going as long as you can.
tr.multi.task: Capture two pieces in one move.
tr.multi.ok: Two at once! That is a multiple jump.
tr.multi.ng: When you can keep jumping, jump to the end.
tr.king.b: A man that reaches the far row becomes a king (marked with a crown). The move ends as soon as it is crowned.
tr.king.task: Advance a white man to the far row to crown it.
tr.king.ng: Move a man onto the top row.
tr.kingmove.b: A king moves one square diagonally forwards or backwards. It can also capture backwards.
tr.kingmove.task: Use the white king to capture the black piece behind it.
tr.kingmove.ng: Move the king backwards to capture.
tr.win.b: You win when all of your opponent's pieces are captured.
tr.win.task: Capture the last black piece and win.
tr.block.b: If it is your opponent's turn and they have no legal move, you win — even if they still have pieces.
tr.block.task: Play the move that leaves the black man with no move.
tr.block.ng: Block the square in front of the black man.
tr.draw.b: When neither side can win, the game is a draw. On this site the game is drawn when the same position occurs three times, or after 40 moves each (80 in all) without a capture or a man move. In king endings, the weaker side can often hold a draw by running to a "double corner" (1 and 5, or 28 and 32).
rt.title: Your rating
rt.desc: Opponents (AI from 15 kyu to 5 dan) are chosen to match your rating (starting at 1000). Usually they are close to your level, sometimes stronger or weaker. Win to go up, lose to go down (Elo; the first 10 games move more). Random colour, 5 minutes + 3 seconds per move. No undo, hints or evaluation during the game (you can review afterwards). Running out of time or leaving counts as a loss. AI ratings are this site's own scale.
rt.noEval: No evaluation during a rated game
rt.abandonQ: A rated game is in progress. Leaving now abandons it and counts as a loss. Continue?
ls.title: Lessons
ls.desc: "Checkers for beginners" for those who have just learned the rules, "Tactics" for winning real games and "Endgames" for finishing them. Each step has 5 problems worth 20 points; 75 points pass. Tactics and endgame problems are verified by the engine, and moves other than the best still score according to how little they lose.
fb.values: Engine value (1.0 = one piece): your move {a} / best {b}
course.basics.sub: Start here once you know the rules: moving, capturing, multiple jumps, crowning and winning, checked with problems.
course.tactics.sub: Checkers games are decided by "shots" — a sacrifice followed by multiple captures. Train finding them, and stopping them.
course.endgame.sub: How to win with few pieces left, and how to hold when you are behind. Verified with the endgame databases.
course.graduate: 🎉 "Checkers for beginners" completed! You are ready to play — try the AI at 15 kyu to 10 kyu first.
op.title: Openings
op.desc: Checkers openings have had names for a long time. The first moves of each line are those of the named opening; after that the moves were chosen by this site's engine after a deep search. Step through them in "Study", then guess the engine's choices in "Practice" (5 problems, 75 points to pass).
op.credit: Opening names and first moves follow the classic classification (e.g. F. Reinfeld, "How to Win at Checkers"). The rest of each line and the evaluations were chosen by this site's engine, thinking seconds to tens of seconds per position, and may differ from perfect play (checkers is a draw with best play; J. Schaeffer et al., 2007).
